name: Professional Trading
goal: Operate like a professional: automate with code, understand derivatives and execution, manage a portfolio of strategies and run trading as a business.
milestones: Code one strategy in C# on QuantConnect LEAN and run a backtest with costs.
Paper trade an options strategy and explain each greek in your position.
Run at least two uncorrelated strategies with a combined risk budget.
Have 6+ months of journaled, plan-following results before scaling capital.

lessons.title: Algorithmic trading with C#
body: Algorithmic trading means a program executes your rules. Benefits: no emotions, perfect consistency, fast backtesting and the ability to watch many markets. Risks: bugs, data errors and over-optimisation.

C# is a first-class language for this. QuantConnect's open-source LEAN engine is written in C# and lets you backtest and live trade stocks, futures, forex, options and crypto with many brokers. NinjaTrader (NinjaScript) and cTrader (cAlgo) also use C#.

This app's code is your starting point: Trading/Indicators.cs shows how SMA, EMA, RSI, MACD and ATR are calculated; Trading/PaperAccount.cs shows how fills, stops, commissions and P/L work; Trading/MarketSimulator.cs shows how synthetic prices are generated. Try writing an automated strategy that trades the simulator.

Production essentials: logging every decision, kill switches, maximum position and loss limits in code, reconciliation of your positions with the broker, and testing with paper accounts before live money.
keyTakeaways: Algorithms remove emotion but add technology risk.
QuantConnect LEAN, NinjaTrader and cTrader all use C#.
Always build kill switches and hard limits into code.
lessons.exercise: Fork this repository and write a class that trades MarketSimulator automatically using the Level 6 trend strategy. Run it on 100 seeds and report average return and drawdown.
readMore: Ernest P. Chan, 'Algorithmic Trading: Winning Strategies and Their Rationale'
Stefan Jansen, 'Machine Learning for Algorithmic Trading'

lessons.title: Options and derivatives
body: A call option gives the right to buy at the strike price before expiry; a put gives the right to sell. Buyers pay a premium and can lose at most that premium. Sellers collect the premium but can face large losses.
Option prices depend on the underlying price, strike, time to expiry, interest rates and implied volatility. The Black-Scholes model is the classic pricing model.
The greeks measure sensitivity: delta (to price), gamma (how delta changes), theta (time decay), vega (to volatility). Professionals manage these exposures rather than just direction.
Defined-risk strategies such as vertical spreads, covered calls and protective puts are the sensible place to start. Never sell naked options until you fully understand the worst case.
keyTakeaways: Calls = right to buy, puts = right to sell.
Know your greeks: delta, gamma, theta, vega.
lessons.exercise: Paper trade a bull call spread. Write down the max profit, max loss and break-even before entering.
readMore: Lawrence G. McMillan, 'Options as a Strategic Investment'

lessons.title: Portfolio of strategies and execution
body: Professionals rarely depend on one strategy. Combining uncorrelated strategies (for example trend following and mean reversion, on different markets) smooths the equity curve and reduces drawdowns.
Set a total risk budget: for example, maximum 5% of capital at risk across all open positions, and allocate risk by volatility so each strategy contributes similarly.

Market microstructure is how orders actually meet: the order book, liquidity, market makers and price impact. Large orders move price, so professionals split them (VWAP, TWAP) and prefer limit orders when possible.
Measure execution quality: compare your fill prices with the price when you decided to trade. Slippage is a cost you can reduce.
keyTakeaways: Execution quality is part of your edge.
lessons.exercise: Run two different strategies in the simulator on the same seed. Would combining them have reduced drawdown?
readMore: Larry Harris, 'Trading and Exchanges: Market Microstructure for Practitioners'

lessons.title: Trading as a business
body: Treat trading like a business with a plan, a budget, records and performance reviews. Track costs: data, software, platform fees, taxes and your time.
Be realistic about returns. Very good professional traders and funds often target 10-30% per year with controlled drawdowns. Promises of 10% per month are marketing or fraud.

Routes to trading professionally include working at a bank or fund, joining a proprietary trading firm, or trading your own capital. Read the rules and costs of funded-account 'challenges' carefully; many are designed so most participants fail.
Know the regulation: market abuse rules (insider trading, manipulation) apply to everyone. Keep tax records of every trade. In Norway, check Finanstilsynet and Skatteetaten guidance.
keyTakeaways: Run it like a business with records and reviews.
Realistic returns are measured per year, not per day.
Know the regulations and tax rules.
lessons.exercise: Write a one-page business plan: capital, monthly costs, target return, max drawdown, and what you will do if you hit it.
readMore: Edwin Lefèvre, 'Reminiscences of a Stock Operator'

quiz.prompt: Which open-source trading engine is written in C#?
quiz.explanation: LEAN is QuantConnect's open-source C# engine for backtesting and live trading.

quiz.prompt: What is the maximum loss for the buyer of a call option?
quiz.explanation: The buyer can only lose what they paid for the option.
Theta is how much value an option loses as time passes.

options: To smooth returns and reduce drawdowns
quiz.explanation: When one strategy struggles, another may do well.

quiz.prompt: A trading course promises 10% profit every month. This is:
quiz.explanation: That is over 200% per year compounded. Very few, if any, achieve it consistently.

quiz.prompt: Which is an essential safety feature in a live trading algorithm?
options: A kill switch and hard loss limits
quiz.explanation: Bugs happen. Hard limits stop a bug from destroying the account.

quiz.prompt: VWAP and TWAP execution are used to:
options: Split large orders to reduce market impact
quiz.explanation: They spread a big order over time to get a better average price.
